prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18.

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B020) because it is the clearest discovery among the shortlisted entries, but the discussion has moved me to the optical lattice clock (B030) as the stronger prize. Six of eight members place it in their top three, and the colleagues who work closest to atomic physics, Lindroth and Kroll, describe a concept (the magic-wavelength proposal) that is original and was then driven to a measurable result: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, independent agreement between laboratories in Japan, the US and Europe, and a stable interpretation. The attribution is the cleanest on the list, with Katori holding the conceptual proposal and early demonstrations and Ye the record accuracy and many-body regime, so no name has to be dropped. The payoff is also the kind of clue from nature I care about as a theorist: millimetre-scale tests of gravitational redshift, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and the road to a new definition of the second. The achievement is mature, with several independent confirmations and no open question about whether the effect exists.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and kind. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize trapped-ion control, so a lattice-clock prize can look like a third award in one metrology lineage. It is also a technology and instrument achievement rather than a new phenomenon, so the discovery content must be argued through the fundamental-physics tests it enables. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and other strontium and ytterbium groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and others) fall outside the two credited names. If the committee reads the prize record as saturated, B020 is the cleaner discovery and B030 is the weaker choice.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that B030 combines the accuracy of single-ion clocks with the statistics of many atoms, that the underlying atomic physics is original, and that neither the 2005 nor the 2012 prize covered lattice clocks themselves.
responses.response: I accept this and it is why I moved B030 up from sixth place. My opening worry was that this is invention with thin discovery content. Your point about light shifts, forbidden transitions and many-body shifts shows the physics is the achievement and not only the engineering. I would still ask the committee to state in the citation what the clocks have enabled, otherwise the metrology-prize-overlap objection stays open. I do not think that objection is strong enough to disqualify the entry.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B030 first as a conceptual invention plus its realization that has changed what can be measured, and he picks Bloch, Zoller and Esslinger for B004, dropping Greiner.
responses.response: I agree on B030 and find the point about millimetre-scale redshift tests and dark-matter searches decisive for me. On B004 I disagree with the three-name cut. Dropping Greiner, whose role in the 2002 Mott transition and the gas microscope is central, is as hard to defend as dropping Esslinger, and your own uncertainty list concedes the allocation is contested. That attribution problem is the reason I keep B004 only as an alternative and not as my preferred prize.

responses.point: Pearce, our chair, ranks IceCube first with Halzen, Karle and Spiering, calls the three-name set workable, and notes that credit between conception, construction and analysis is not fully settled.
responses.response: We agree on B020's scientific merit, and I now think including Spiering is right for a three-name set. I would not push it as the preferred prize. Its opening support is thin (two first places, three rankings), the source population is still unresolved, and the credit split between AMANDA founders, IceCube leaders and the collaboration remains an open question. I keep it as my first alternative and would support it if the committee wants an astrophysics discovery, but B030 is cleaner on attribution.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED (B029) first, disclosing his closeness to the field, and notes that Wallraff is missing from the credited names and that the 2025 prize touched neighbouring superconducting-circuit physics.
responses.response: I take your candour about proximity seriously, and the architecture's importance for superconducting processors is not in doubt. I still hesitate on B029 for two reasons you raise yourself. A trio without Wallraff leaves out a decisive experimental contributor, and the 2025 award makes a second superconducting-circuit prize this soon hard to justify. I would let it mature before putting it ahead of B030.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards frequency metrology as already sufficiently honoured by the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether other lattice-clock groups outside the credited names should be considered, and whether Katori and Ye is the final attribution.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second before awarding.
I am working from recalled facts rather than independently checked ones.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are not linked to B030, B020 or B004.
